Melanoma.description: Melanoma is the most serious form of skin cancer, originating in pigment-producing melanocytes. Early detection and prompt surgical excision are critical for optimal prognosis.
symptoms: Asymmetrical shape with irregular, notched, or blurred borders
Varied colors within the same lesion (tan, brown, black, red, white, or blue)
Diameter larger than 6mm (pencil eraser size), though can be smaller
Evolution in size, shape, color, or elevation over time
New itching, tenderness, oozing, or bleeding in a mole
causes: Intermittent severe UV radiation exposure (sunburns)
Genetic mutations (CDKN2A, BRAF)
High mole count or dysplastic nevus syndrome
Fair skin, light hair, and personal/family history of skin cancer
precautions: Perform monthly self-skin exams using the ABCDE rule
Apply broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen daily and reapply every 2 hours
Avoid tanning beds and direct peak sun exposure (10 AM - 4 PM)
Wear protective clothing, wide-brimmed hats, and UV-blocking sunglasses
warning_signs: Rapidly growing mole or dark spot
Lesion that bleeds, crusts, or refuses to heal
New pigmented stripe under a fingernail or toenail
Melanoma.doctor_advice: Immediate in-person evaluation by a board-certified dermatologist is strongly recommended for dermoscopy and diagnostic biopsy.

Basal Cell Carcinoma.description: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) is the most common form of skin cancer, arising in the basal layer of the epidermis. It grows slowly and rarely metastasizes but can cause localized tissue destruction.
symptoms: Pearly, translucent, or waxy bump with visible tiny blood vessels (telangiectasias)
Flat, firm, scar-like lesion that appears pale yellow or white
Sore that bleeds, oozes, or crusts, heals, and then recurs
Pink growth with a rolled border and central crust or indentation
causes: Cumulative long-term ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sun exposure
Use of indoor tanning equipment
Older age and fair skin types (Fitzpatrick I-II)
precautions: Protect sun-exposed areas (face, neck, ears, scalp) with daily broad-spectrum SPF 30+
Inspect persistent non-healing bumps or pink patches regularly
Schedule annual full-body skin checks with a dermatologist
warning_signs: A sore that does not heal within 4 weeks
A bump that easily bleeds with minimal trauma
Basal Cell Carcinoma.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist for clinical evaluation, skin biopsy, and treatment options such as Mohs surgery or excision.

Actinic Keratosis.description: Actinic Keratosis (AK) is a rough, scaly precancerous skin lesion caused by chronic UV damage. If left untreated, a small percentage may progress to squamous cell carcinoma.
symptoms: Rough, dry, scaly, or sandpaper-like patch of skin
Flat or slightly raised lesion, ranging from skin-colored to reddish-brown
Occasional itching, burning, or tenderness when rubbed
causes: Chronic, long-term exposure to sunlight or tanning beds
Cumulative UV damage over decades
precautions: Strict sun protection using broad-spectrum SPF 50+ sunscreen
Wear sun-protective hats and UV clothing during outdoor activities
Avoid outdoor activities during peak UV index hours
warning_signs: Rapid thickening, enlargement, or ulceration of the lesion
Development of a hard, horn-like projection (cutaneous horn)
Actinic Keratosis.doctor_advice: Dermatological evaluation is recommended for field therapy (cryotherapy, topical 5-FU, or photodynamic therapy).

Nevus.description: A nevus (mole) is a benign melanocytic growth appearing as a small, circumscribed skin spot. Most common moles are harmless, though changing moles require evaluation.
symptoms: Uniform tan, brown, black, or skin-colored spot
Round or oval shape with smooth, distinct borders
Flat (macule) or slightly raised (papule)
Consistent appearance over long periods
causes: Proliferation of melanocyte pigment cells
Genetic predisposition and childhood sun exposure
precautions: Track mole appearance, size, and shape periodically
Apply daily sunscreen to prevent UV-induced dysplastic changes
Seek medical opinion if a mole develops irregular features
warning_signs: Development of ABCDE characteristics (asymmetry, border irregularity, color shift)
New onset of pain, itching, bleeding, or elevation
Nevus.doctor_advice: Benign moles require no treatment, but any new or evolving mole should be examined by a dermatologist.

Benign Keratosis.description: Benign Keratosis encompasses non-cancerous skin growths such as seborrheic keratosis, solar lentigines, and lichen planus-like keratosis that develop with age and sun exposure.
symptoms: Waxy, elevated, 'stuck-on' appearance
Color ranging from light tan to dark brown or black
Rough, verrucous, or velvety surface texture
Asymptomatic or mild friction irritation
causes: Natural skin aging processes
Genetic predisposition
Cumulative UV exposure (for solar lentigines)
precautions: Avoid scratching or picking at raised lesions to prevent secondary infection
Use mild cleansers and moisturizers on affected areas
warning_signs: Rapid change in color, ulceration, or spontaneous bleeding
Difficulty distinguishing the growth from a malignant melanoma
Benign Keratosis.doctor_advice: Benign lesions do not require removal unless inflamed or cosmetically desired. Dermoscopy helps rule out malignancy.

Seborrheic Keratosis.description: Seborrheic Keratosis is a very common, non-cancerous skin growth that typically appears in middle-aged and older adults. It has a characteristic 'stuck-on' waxy appearance.
symptoms: Round or oval waxy plaque appearing glued to the skin
Surface may be smooth or rough and crumbly
Color varies from light yellow-tan to dark brown or black
Common on chest, back, shoulders, face, and neck
causes: Epidermal cell maturation changes
Familial inheritance (genetic predisposition)
precautions: Prevent snagging on clothing or jewelry
Do not attempt to scrape or cut off growths at home
warning_signs: Sudden eruptive appearance of multiple new lesions (Leser-Trélat sign)
Bleeding or severe inflammation following irritation
Seborrheic Keratosis.doctor_advice: Harmless benign growths. Cryotherapy or curettage can be performed by a dermatologist if symptomatic.

Dermatofibroma.description: Dermatofibroma is a common, benign fibrous skin nodule often occurring on the lower legs, frequently developing after minor trauma like a bug bite or razor nick.
symptoms: Small, hard, firm button-like nodule beneath the skin surface
Color ranges from pinkish-red to reddish-brown
'Dimple sign': lesion dimples inward when pinched from the sides
Usually asymptomatic, occasionally mildly itchy or tender
causes: Fibroblastic reaction to minor skin trauma (arthropod bite, puncture)
precautions: Avoid shaving directly over raised nodules to prevent nicks
Monitor for stability in size and firm texture
warning_signs: Rapid growth, bleeding, or color change
Dermatofibroma.doctor_advice: Benign lesion requiring no treatment. Surgical excision is available if painful or irritated.

Vascular Lesion.description: Vascular Lesions include benign blood vessel malformations and proliferations such as cherry angiomas, telangiectasias, pyogenic granulomas, and port-wine stains.
symptoms: Bright red, purple, or bluish spots or elevated papules
Lesions blanch (fade) under direct pressure
Pyogenic granulomas bleed easily with minor contact
causes: Endothelial cell proliferation or vessel dilation
Hormonal changes, trauma, or congenital vascular development
precautions: Avoid picking or pressing aggressively on vascular growths
Apply direct pressure if bleeding occurs after minor friction
warning_signs: Recurrent, profuse bleeding from a rapidly enlarging red nodule
Sudden darkening or irregular border expansion
Vascular Lesion.doctor_advice: Dermatological laser therapy or electrocautery can effectively treat symptomatic vascular lesions.

Psoriasis.description: Psoriasis is a chronic autoimmune condition that speeds up skin cell life cycles, causing skin cells to build up rapidly and form thick, silvery scaly plaques.
symptoms: Raised, red skin patches covered with thick, silvery scales
Dry, cracked skin that may bleed
Itching, burning, or soreness around plaques
Common on elbows, knees, scalp, lower back, and nails
causes: Immune system dysregulation (T-cell activation)
Genetic factors combined with environmental triggers (stress, infections, cold weather)
precautions: Keep skin thoroughly moisturized with thick ointments or creams
Avoid skin trauma, harsh soaps, smoking, and excessive alcohol
Manage emotional stress and maintain moderate, safe sun exposure
warning_signs: Widespread body redness and skin peeling (erythrodermic psoriasis)
Joint pain, stiffness, or swelling (psoriatic arthritis)
Psoriasis.doctor_advice: Consult a dermatologist for individualized treatment including topical steroids, phototherapy, or biologic therapies.

Eczema.description: Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by dry, intensely itchy, red, and irritated skin patches due to an impaired skin barrier.
symptoms: Intense itching (pruritus), especially at night
Red, dry, crusty, or leathery skin patches
Small raised bumps that may leak fluid when scratched
Common on flexural areas (elbow creases, back of knees, wrists, neck)
causes: Skin barrier dysfunction (FLG filaggrin gene variants)
Immune system hypersensitivity
Triggers like dry air, harsh soaps, dust mites, pet dander, and stress
precautions: Apply ceramide-rich moisturizers immediately after lukewarm baths
Use mild, fragrance-free, soap-free body washes
Wear soft, breathable cotton clothing and avoid wool
Keep fingernails trimmed to minimize scratch damage
warning_signs: Signs of secondary bacterial infection (yellow crusting, pus, worsening redness)
Widespread painful blistering (eczema herpeticum)
Eczema.doctor_advice: A dermatologist can prescribe topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, or targeted biologics.

Acne.description: Acne Vulgaris is a common inflammatory disorder of the pilosebaceous unit, resulting in comedones, papules, pustules, and sometimes deeper nodulocystic lesions.
symptoms: Non-inflammatory comedones (blackheads and whiteheads)
Inflammatory red papules and pus-filled pustules
Deep, painful nodules or cysts under the skin
Common on face, forehead, chest, upper back, and shoulders
causes: Excess sebum production stimulated by androgens
Hyperkeratinization leading to clogged pores
Cutibacterium acnes (C. acnes) bacterial proliferation
Inflammatory response
precautions: Wash face twice daily with a gentle, non-comedogenic cleanser
Avoid squeezing, popping, or picking at pimples to prevent scarring
Use non-comedogenic sunscreen and oil-free cosmetics
Trial OTC salicylic acid or benzoyl peroxide treatments
warning_signs: Severe deep nodular/cystic acne causing permanent scarring
Sudden severe flare accompanied by fever (acne fulminans)
Acne.doctor_advice: Persistent or severe acne should be managed by a dermatologist with topical retinoids, oral antibiotics, or isotretinoin.

Rosacea.description: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory vascular skin condition affecting primarily the central facial skin, leading to persistent redness, flushing, visible blood vessels, and papules.
symptoms: Facial flushing and persistent redness across nose and cheeks
Visible small blood vessels (telangiectasias)
Swollen red bumps and pustules resembling acne (papulopustular rosacea)
Eye burning, dryness, or stinging (ocular rosacea)
Skin thickening on the nose (rhinophyma)
causes: Neurovascular dysregulation and innate immune hyperreactivity
Environmental triggers: spicy foods, hot beverages, alcohol, extreme temperatures, sun, stress
precautions: Identify and avoid personal flare triggers
Apply gentle, physical (mineral) broad-spectrum SPF 30+ daily
Use mild, non-irritating facial cleansers; avoid harsh scrubs and alcohol toners
warning_signs: Eye symptoms such as pain, blurred vision, or severe dryness
Progressive thickening of skin on the nose
Rosacea.doctor_advice: Dermatological care can manage symptoms using topical ivermectin, metronidazole, laser therapy, or oral antibiotics.

Vitiligo.description: Vitiligo is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system targets and destroys functional melanocytes, resulting in smooth, depigmented white patches of skin.
symptoms: Loss of skin color in chalk-white or milky-white patches
Premature whitening or graying of hair, eyelashes, or eyebrows
Depigmentation around body openings (mouth, eyes, nostrils)
Symmetrical distribution across hands, face, knees, and feet
causes: Autoimmune destruction of melanocyte cells
Genetic vulnerability combined with oxidative stress
precautions: Protect depigmented skin with SPF 50+ sunscreen as white skin burns easily
Avoid skin friction, abrasions, or physical injury (Koebner phenomenon)
warning_signs: Rapidly spreading depigmentation patches across new body regions
Vitiligo.doctor_advice: A dermatologist can evaluate repigmentation treatments including topical corticosteroids, JAK inhibitors, and narrowband UVB phototherapy.

Warts.description: Warts are benign, contagious skin growths caused by localized infection of keratinocytes with the Human Papillomavirus (HPV).
symptoms: Small, grainy, rough flesh-colored or pink bumps
Surface dotted with tiny black pinpoint dots (clotted capillaries)
Common on fingers, hands, elbows, and soles of feet (plantar warts)
May be tender under pressure on soles of feet
causes: Infection with Human Papillomavirus (HPV) strains via direct contact or fomites
precautions: Avoid picking, scratching, or shaving over warts to prevent viral spread
Wear sandals in public showers and pool decks
Do not share towels, nail clippers, or personal items
warning_signs: Warts that bleed, become painful, or change appearance rapidly
Warts in individuals with weakened immune systems
Warts.doctor_advice: OTC salicylic acid preparations can be tried. Persistent warts can be treated by a dermatologist with cryotherapy or laser treatment.

Impetigo.description: Impetigo is a highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection most commonly affecting infants and young children, characterized by honey-colored crusts.
symptoms: Red sores that quickly rupture, ooze for days, and form honey-colored crusts
Fluid-filled blisters (bullous impetigo)
Itching and mild soreness around nose, mouth, and hands
causes: Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes bacterial entry into broken skin
precautions: Wash affected areas gently with mild soap and water, then cover loosely
Wash clothing, linens, and towels daily in hot water
Keep infected children home from school until contagiousness passes
warning_signs: Spreading redness, warmth, or fever indicating deeper infection (cellulitis)
Renal symptoms (dark urine) following streptococcal skin infection
Impetigo.doctor_advice: Impetigo requires prompt evaluation by a healthcare provider for prescription topical mupirocin or oral antibiotics.

Tinea.description: Tinea refers to superficial fungal infections of the keratinized tissues (skin, hair, nails) caused by dermatophyte fungi.
symptoms: Itchy, scaly, reddish circular or spreading skin patches
Active leading edge with central clearing
Maceration and peeling between toes (tinea pedis / athlete's foot)
Chafing, red-brown rash in groin folds (tinea cruris / jock itch)
causes: Dermatophyte fungal growth (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton)
Warmth, humidity, tight clothing, and friction
precautions: Keep affected skin clean and completely dry
Change socks and underwear daily
Use OTC antifungal creams (terbinafine, clotrimazole) as directed
Avoid sharing footwear, towels, or athletic gear
warning_signs: Spreading inflammation, severe pain, or purulent pus discharge
Tinea.doctor_advice: Persistent fungal infections should be evaluated by a physician for prescription topical or oral antifungal medication.

Ringworm.description: Ringworm (Tinea Corporis) is a superficial dermatophyte fungal infection affecting body skin, creating characteristic ring-shaped scaly lesions.
symptoms: Ring-shaped red, raised scaly border with clearer skin in the middle
Persistent localized itching and scaling
Lesions expand outward slowly
causes: Direct skin-to-skin contact with infected humans, pets (cats/dogs), or soil
precautions: Apply OTC antifungal cream extending 1 inch beyond lesion borders
Have pets checked by a veterinarian if they show hair loss or scaling
Avoid scratching to prevent secondary bacterial infection
warning_signs: Extensive body coverage or failure to improve after 2 weeks of OTC antifungal treatment
Ringworm.doctor_advice: Consult a healthcare provider for confirmation (KOH prep) and prescription strength antifungal care.

Contact Dermatitis.description: Contact Dermatitis is an inflammatory skin reaction triggered by direct contact with irritants (irritant contact dermatitis) or allergens (allergic contact dermatitis).
symptoms: Red rash, swelling, and localized skin warmth
Intense itching, burning, or stinging sensations
Blisters or tiny bumps that ooze and crust
Rash confined to area of substance contact
causes: Irritants: harsh soaps, detergents, chemicals, friction
Allergens: poison ivy/oak (urushiol), nickel, fragrances, latex, topical preservatives
precautions: Wash skin immediately after suspected exposure to remove offending agent
Apply cool compresses and bland fragrance-free moisturizers
Use OTC 1% hydrocortisone cream short-term for localized itching
Identify and avoid contact with known trigger substances
warning_signs: Widespread severe blistering, facial swelling, or rash near eyes/mouth
Signs of bacterial infection (pus, increasing redness and warmth)
Contact Dermatitis.doctor_advice: A dermatologist can perform patch testing to identify specific allergens and prescribe potent topical steroids.

Lupus.description: Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (CLE) is an autoimmune skin condition causing sun-sensitive skin lesions, discoid scarring plaques, or a classic butterfly rash across the face.
symptoms: Red, malar (butterfly) rash across nose and cheeks
Coin-shaped (discoid) scaly, thick red plaques that leave scars
Extreme photosensitivity (flares triggered by sun exposure)
Hair loss (alopecia) and mouth sores
causes: Autoimmune response targeting skin cells
Genetic susceptibility triggered by UV radiation
precautions: Strict daily sun protection with SPF 50+ and broad-brimmed hats
Avoid sun lamps, fluorescent light exposure, and indoor tanning
Do not smoke as smoking reduces treatment efficacy
warning_signs: Joint pain, fever, fatigue, or chest pain indicating systemic lupus (SLE)
Lupus.doctor_advice: Requires ongoing management by a dermatologist and rheumatologist with antimalarial drugs (hydroxychloroquine) and topical anti-inflammatories.

Urticaria.description: Urticaria (Hives) is a vascular skin reaction characterized by transient, itchy raised welts (wheals) caused by mast cell histamine release.
symptoms: Raised, intensely itchy red or skin-colored welts (wheals)
Blanch (turn white) when pressed
Lesions change location rapidly, disappearing in one area and appearing elsewhere
Individual welts resolve within 24 hours without leaving scars
causes: Histamine release triggered by food, medication, viral infection, insect stings, stress, or physical pressure
precautions: Avoid known allergic triggers, hot baths, and tight clothing
Take non-drowsy OTC antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine)
Apply cool compresses to soothe itchy skin
warning_signs: Difficulty breathing, swallowing, tongue/throat swelling, or dizziness (anaphylaxis - Call 911 immediately)
Individual welts that persist in one spot over 24 hours or leave bruising
Urticaria.doctor_advice: Emergency care is required if anaphylaxis occurs. Chronic hives (>6 weeks) require allergy and dermatological evaluation.
